narrative_summary: Supplement: ADHD groups showed more media time and more severe PUI than controls. Age group and informant did not change results after sensitivity analyses.

Clinician-diagnosed GD samples showed ADHD rates of 12.5%, 32.7% and 83.3%; one case-control study found ADHD 13 times more likely with GD.

Non-clinical ADHD vs non-ADHD subgroup prints g = 0.630 with 95% CI [0.530, 0.968], which looks inconsistent (possible typo). Left out under the 12-finding cap: hyperactivity/impulsivity clinical r 0.253 (k 10, n 1393, 0.157-0.344) and non-clinical r 0.271 (k 19, n 30,870, 0.226-0.316), Table 6. Not recorded: SEM meta-analysis (hyperactivity/impulsivity r = 0.28 [0.22, 0.34]; inattention r = 0.33 [0.27, 0.38]; heterogeneity >95%); informant, country, tool and addiction-type subgroups. Striking moderators: inattention-GD correlation larger in problematic internet use among gamers than GD-only studies (0.374 vs 0.288, Q = 8.636, p = 0.003); gender ratio coefficient 0.0018 (p = 0.033); data collection year predicted ADHD vs non-ADHD g (0.0528, p < 0.001). Mean age and study quality not significant moderators. Table 1 is scrambled in the text file. Funding/conflict text is partly out of order and truncated in the file. No outcomes outside the condition list.

narrative_summary: Across 223 student studies, PIU correlated moderately with depressive symptoms (r = 0.313, 131 studies), anxiety (r = 0.277, 67 studies) and other mental health outcomes (r = 0.289, 76 studies); the depressive symptoms association was stronger in undergraduates (r = 0.353) than secondary students (r = 0.281) and in more recent studies.

narrative_summary: Across 30 longitudinal studies, GD predicted later depression and emotional (mixed) symptoms but not anxiety; depression, anxiety and emotional symptoms predicted later GD. Partial correlations were small (around 0.07). Excluding Chinese studies made depression-to-GD and anxiety-to-GD non-significant; excluding poor-quality studies changed nothing.

author_conclusion: GD shows reciprocal longitudinal associations with depression, emotional (mixed) symptoms and life satisfaction; anxiety and loneliness predict later GD but GD does not predict anxiety; effects are small (or medium), observational, and of uncertain causal and practical relevance.

Sample counts overlap or conflict: 52 general population plus 7 clinical plus 10 college/athlete studies exceed 54. Text says eight studies had more females than males but cites two. All studies are called cross-sectional, yet the set includes telephone interviews over 2002–2008, a retrospective chart review, repeated cross-sectional surveys and data from a longitudinal project (Orlowski). Liu et al. (2021) is in the cross-sectional appraisal table but described as longitudinal in Table 3. Tobacco range lower bound '20.09%' appears to be Brandao et al.'s tobacco cOR = 20.09 misreported as a percentage; '78-88%' comes from a high-risk/tobacco-smoker latent class (Seproo). Alcohol range lower bound 43.9% appears to be alcohol use disorder among daily gamers (Wang). Polysubstance 'four studies (18.2%)' percentage base unclear. Ranges recorded with estimate null because CI fields are reserved for confidence intervals; range bounds are in the label. Stimulant 'prevalence around 4.9%' is a single-study figure (Ip et al.), not recorded. 'Sample sizes ranged from 64 to 3,939' conflicts with Moreno et al. N = 6,000 in Table 3. Mbarki et al. results in Table 3 duplicate Mannikko et al. figures (35.3%, 7.0%, 10.1%), possible copy error. Text cites Wartberg et al. (2023) but table lists Wartberg et al. (2025). Several Table 3 studies report null or inverse associations (e.g., Sucha et al., Turhan Gurbuz et al., Borges et al. 2023, Seproo et al.), which the narrative does not count. extraction_notes: Classified as meta-analysis because a random-effects pooled r is reported, although the title says systematic review. Only one pooled estimate, combining depression and anxiety; per-condition results recorded as study counts. Q = 494.206 with df = 21 for 15 studies implies more effect sizes than studies (dependence not addressed). Study [34] is counted negative for depression but positive for anxiety; [38] positive for depression but negative for anxiety; 'negative associations' may mean inverse or non-significant, unclear. Heterogeneity bands in Methods overlap (moderate 30-60%, substantial 50-90%). Forest and funnel plots (Figs 2-3) and Tables 1-3 not available in text. PSMU prevalence 22.4 to 23.7% (three studies) is an online-side figure, not recorded; PSMU-time spent association (0.286 < r < 0.583, three studies) not recorded. Mediators (stress, generalized trust, perceived social support, fear of COVID-19) and outcomes outside the list (stress, psychological distress, loneliness, wellbeing) not recorded. Authors note larger effect sizes in academic high-stress settings [39, 41, 42] without a formal subgroup analysis. No age-group or clinical/community subgroup analysis.

narrative_summary: No pooled estimates. Across 13 studies, all four exposure domains (time spent, activity, investment, addiction) correlated with depression, anxiety and distress, but findings were mixed: time-spent studies conflicted (null, inverse and positive results), activity findings were mixed, while the three addiction studies all reported positive associations with depression. 12 of 13 studies were cross-sectional.

author_conclusion: Social media use (time, activity, investment, addiction) is correlated with adolescent depression, anxiety and psychological distress, but the relationship is complex, multifactorial and not shown to be causal; longitudinal cohort and qualitative research is needed.

narrative_summary: No counts or pooled figures. The most consistent finding across the 50 studies was that doomscrolling was positively associated with anxiety, depression, stress and psychological distress; several studies reported post-traumatic stress symptoms; a bidirectional, self-reinforcing cycle between distress and doomscrolling was described. Evidence mostly cross-sectional.
narrative_locator: Results, p. 167: 'Doomscrolling was positively associated with increased levels of anxiety, depression, stress, and psychological distress. Several studies also reported associations with post-traumatic stress symptoms'
author_conclusion: Doomscrolling is a multidimensional, crisis-driven behaviour consistently associated with anxiety, depression, stress and lower well-being, shaped by individual vulnerabilities and platform design; evidence is fragmented and mostly cross-sectional, needing standardized measures and longitudinal, experimental and intervention studies.

narrative_summary: Nearly all studies were cross-sectional self-report surveys of community or student samples. Cyberchondria correlated with health anxiety (an included meta-analysis: r = 0.62), with OCD symptom scores (moderate correlations; constructs distinct), and with problematic internet use in several studies. Anxiety sensitivity and intolerance of uncertainty findings were inconsistent. No reliable prevalence data; no treatment studies.

author_conclusion: Cyberchondria is a clinically relevant transdiagnostic compulsive behavioural syndrome, closely related to problematic internet use and usually presenting with health anxiety, hypochondriasis and/or OCD; evidence is mostly cross-sectional self-report from community samples, and further study is needed.

narrative_summary: All 15 studies found harmful effects of viewing online self-harm images: 8 reported triggering or escalating self-harm, 11 emotional changes raising self-harm likelihood, 6 increased self-harm urges or suicidal ideation. Cap of 12 findings reached; left out: protective identity impact (4 studies), harmful physiological impact (1 study) and protective physiological impact (1 study), protective engagement (no count given). Only two quantitative studies tested contagion, with contradictory results (Arendt et al. 2019 found prediction of self-harm and suicidality 1 month later; Brown et al. 2018 found no clustering). Single-study figures not recorded (e.g. 32.5% imitated self-harm after seeing it on Instagram). Internal inconsistency: text says 32 of 86 hopeful images in Seko and Lewis (2018), while Table 2 gives n = 21 with 132 reblogs. Most quantitative studies were low or medium quality; most qualitative studies high quality. Outcomes such as mood decline, emotional disturbance, hopelessness and reasons for living are folded into the emotional/cognitive counts.

Heavy-use paragraph says 'Four articles reported associations...' then 'three articles found an association [53-55]', with Kim [57] described separately; recorded 3 of 4 as printed. Sampasa-Kanyinga 2015a (heavy SNS use with ideation and attempts) is discussed under cyberbullying. Lee 2017 concerns video gaming/nonacademic computer use and Twenge 2019 electronic device use, not social media specifically. Table 2 calls the Kim association 'strong and negative' though OR = 1.36 indicates higher odds; Kim cyberbullying CI printed '1.222.59' in text vs '1.22-2.59' in Table 2. Niederkrotenthaler listed as Australia in Table 1 and Austria in Table 2. Conclusion gives the period as 2015-2019. Single-study effects (e.g., aOR 5.93, OR 1.79, 14.6% excess suicides) not recorded; mediation by cybervictimization (2 articles) not recorded as a finding. Single-study effects quoted in the review (e.g., DS OR = 3.62, RR = 1.25; anhedonia OR = 1.33) not recorded. online_exposures: ChatGPT / LLM chatbot use for mental health support
population_notes: No age restriction stated; lay users (Reddit and social media), psychiatric inpatients (n = 12), outpatients (Saudi Arabia), counseling trainees and educators, students, chemo-naive cancer patients, ChatGPT outputs on vignettes; child/adolescent perspective pieces; Asia, Middle East, Europe, North America.
primary_designs: 21 empirical (surveys, interviews, pilot trials, ethnographies, experimental simulations; two randomized trials) and 13 conceptual/commentary articles
narrative_summary: No pooled or counted results. Suicide-risk vignette and social-media screening studies found ChatGPT under-identified suicide risk or stratified it inconsistently versus clinicians. Public self-help use studies flagged privacy, boundary and over-reliance risks. Benefit signals came from single studies: reduced anxiety/depression in one RCT outside psychiatry, short-term anxiety reduction in one experiment.
narrative_locator: Discussion, Principal Findings: 'models tend to under-identify suicide risk or stratify it inconsistently relative to clinicians'; Results, Public/Self-Help: 'participants and observers flagged privacy, boundary, and over-reliance risks in open communities'
author_conclusion: Evidence supports ChatGPT as an adjunct, not a replacement, mainly for scaffolded training and low-risk psychoeducation; safety-critical tasks such as suicide-risk assessment remain unreliable, requiring human oversight, scope messaging, privacy-preserving defaults and escalation pathways.

author_conclusion: Online romance scams are an emerging, largely unrecognized phenomenon; identifying psychological characteristics of victims and scammers (e.g., neuroticism, romantic idealization, impulsivity) can define at-risk profiles and guide prevention, screening and victim support.

Errors found: PSMU text says 'Out of 10 studies, all reported' but lists 9 citations; Choi et al. 2015 depression beta is -0.215 in Table 2 yet cited as a depression risk factor; Gao et al. 2021 depression (0.184) and anxiety (0.194) coded 'S (-)' in Table 2 but cited as risk factors; Jasso-Medrano & Lopez-Rosales found suicidal ideation negatively related to PSMU (-0.21). Quality counts do not add up (56 good = 47.9%, 30 fair = 52.1%, of 117). Text says 10 PSU, 5 PSMU and 1 IGD factors but also '17 predictive factors' and 'four associated with PSMU'. Rozgonjuk et al. 2018 is listed as prospective in Table 2 but Rozgonjuk et al. 2019 is named as longitudinal in text. 117 rows include studies counted in two groups (e.g., Yuan et al., 2021 in PSU and IGD), so unique studies are fewer than 117. extraction_notes: Authors call this a 'descriptive systematic overview' (Grant and Booth) and explicitly chose it over a systematic review; classed here as systematic review without meta-analysis, 'other review' is a defensible alternative. No pooled, median, range or study-count results are stated across studies, so findings is empty; risk factors are reported as lists of citations only. Not recorded: background prevalence ranges in the Introduction (e.g. young people 1% to 10.4%, older adults up to 10.6%, veterans 0.2% to 10.7%) and single-study figures (70% versus 46% Axis I comorbidity in veterans; 'up to 3 times more likely'). Psychosis and schizophrenia (a map cell) are not mentioned anywhere in the text; nearest are 'Axis I psychiatric disorders', 'greater mental disabilities' and 'mood swings'. PTSD: associated with gambling in veterans (Whiting et al., 2016) but Biddle et al. (2005) found no significant relationship with PTSD, anxiety, depression or alcohol use. One older-adult study reports the reverse direction (gambling followed by incident generalized anxiety and substance use disorders). Online-specific exposures appear only as risk factors: online gambling (women), video games with simulated gambling, social casinos and gambling advertising (youth). Other conditions named as risk factors: higher ADHD scores, childhood hyperactivity and learning disorders (youth), traumatic brain injury (veterans), Parkinson's medication, suicide attempts more likely in Maori disordered gamblers. Non-counted outcomes also mentioned: loneliness, low self-esteem, negative affectivity, stress, poor coping, boredom. PRISMA: identified Youth 3169, Indigenous 100, Older 669, Prisoners 53, Women 2532, Poverty 114, Veterans 81; 6718 screened on title; 2398 excluded (title/duplicate); 4320 assessed for eligibility; 4048 full text excluded; 257* included (Youth 100, Indigenous 40, Older 32, Prisoners 18, Women 47, Poverty 23, Veterans 12; asterisk: articles counted in more than one group). Risk-factor studies limited post hoc to 2000 onwards; older-adult prevalence studies to 2013 onwards. Methods say the single-reviewer title stage removed only duplicates, but the flow chart labels these exclusions 'title / duplicate'. Source file is a manuscript version with EndNote field codes and the reference list still present; it has no funding or declaration sections.

narrative_summary: Of 22 studies on body image, 19 reported adverse associations with dating app use (body dissatisfaction 8 of 14 positive). Disordered eating 6 of 10 positive. Of 29 studies on mental health and wellbeing, 14 reported adverse associations; depression 4 of 12 and anxiety 3 of 5 positive. Mostly cross-sectional.
narrative_locator: 3.3.2 Mental health and wellbeing; Tables 1 and 2: 'Across all included studies that measured mental health and wellbeing (n = 29), 48.3% (n = 14) reported correlations between dating app use and adverse'
author_conclusion: Dating app use appears to harm users' body image, mental health and wellbeing; app design should be changed to reduce harms, regulation such as age or time limits considered, and longitudinal and experimental research conducted.
rob_tool_used: Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT; Hong et al., 2018), two independent reviewers

amstar2.notes: 1: population (dating app users), exposure (dating app use), outcomes (body image, mental health, wellbeing); comparator implicit (non-users or levels of use). 2: prospectively registered on OSF; deviations not addressed (rated PY per rules). 4: six databases, strategy in Appendix A with librarian, reference lists and citations searched; English only not justified; no grey literature or expert contact. 5: two independent reviewers, kappa 0.83 and 0.92. 6: two reviewers extracted data. 9: MMAT by two independent reviewers (kappa 0.91). 13: notes mostly high-quality studies and that cross-sectional designs preclude causation; judgment call. 14: heterogeneity of constructs and instruments discussed, subpopulations considered.

conflicts: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
extraction_notes: No meta-analysis (heterogeneity of constructs and instruments). Left out of findings: body esteem (1 study; Table 1 and text say significant negative, but Appendix B says Harren 2021 found problematic online dating positively correlated with body esteem); combined mental health and wellbeing count (14 of 29 adverse; mixes counted conditions with self-esteem, mood, life satisfaction, stress); design subsets (body image 14 of 16 quantitative cross-sectional; mental health 15 of 26 cross-sectional); correlates linked with use (depression with perceived rejection n = 2, dating app facilitated sexual violence n = 1, ghosting n = 1, low perceived popularity n = 1; anxiety with online dating debut n = 1 and sexual violence n = 1). Not recorded (outside condition list): self-esteem, stress, mood, life satisfaction. Number inconsistencies: abstract 48.6% (n = 14) vs text 48.3% (n = 14); section 3.2 says 62.2% (n = 28) studies on mental health and wellbeing vs n = 29 in 3.3.2 and abstract 64.4% (n = 29); abstract 'Over 85% (n = 19)' vs 86.4%; body image disturbance listed twice in 3.3.1 (n = 3 and n = 1); limitations say two longitudinal studies vs 4 in results; discussion says 90% published from 2020 vs 86.7% (n = 39). Unhealthy weight control behaviours k = 4 read from Table 1 (no [−] or [0] entries). Map cell 'Disability general' has no matching finding. Appendix B shows a few samples starting at 16 or 17 years and up to 75 despite the reported 18 to 72 range.

population_notes: Dating app users and nonusers, many university students; most samples from the United States; ages 13 to 80, many 18 to 35; of 32 samples, 19 gender-balanced, 9 female-dominated, 4 male-dominated; samples had diverse exclusion criteria (psychopathology excluded in some). Sample sizes 64 to 4057.
primary_designs: Of 32 studies in 29 reports: 29 cross-sectional surveys, 3 randomized experiments
narrative_summary: The review inventoried correlates examined, without reporting direction or significance. Of 29 papers, 11 examined mood and emotional issues (including depressive mood, mental distress, suicidal ideation), 9 examined anxieties; one study each assessed substance use and urges for disordered eating. No cross-study association results were reported.
narrative_locator: Results, Adverse Correlates of Problematized Online Dating (Mood and Emotional Issues; Anxieties): 'A form of anxiety, for example, social or attachment-related anxiety, or fear of being single, was examined in 9 papers.'
author_conclusion: Definitions of problematic dating app use are ambiguous and common scales conflate use with its harms; research is dominated by user motives and single-time-point surveys. Valid measures separating use from outcomes and experimental and longitudinal designs are needed.
rob_tool_used: none reported

amstar2.notes: 1: population unrestricted, exposure problematized dating app use, outcomes adverse correlates; descriptive questions, no comparator. 2: PROSPERO CRD42024601803; one deviation (3 mere-use reports included despite excluding user vs nonuser comparisons) explained. 4: 16 databases, full search string, reference lists searched; peer-reviewed only, English and German, no grey literature. 5: two authors screened individually, disagreements discussed. 6: two researchers 'extracted the data and regularly discussed'; contributions list SD as supporting, so independent duplicate extraction unclear. 8: Tables S1 to S4 in Multimedia Appendix 1 (not in text file) described as giving country, sample, definitions, measures, correlates, design. 13: no individual-study appraisal, though field-level design and measurement weaknesses are discussed at length; judgment call. 14: heterogeneity of definitions, samples and exclusion criteria discussed.

Online bullying victimization and perpetration examined in one paper and trolling in one. Abstract states using apps for sexual motivations and relationship-seeking was linked to adverse correlates, without counts. Correlates outside the condition list (joviality, sadness, alexithymia, love addiction, self-esteem, sleep quality, compulsive sexual behavior, personality) not recorded. No risk of bias appraisal.

narrative_summary: Positive interactions, social support and social connectedness on SNSs were consistently related to lower depression and anxiety; negative interactions, social comparison and problematic SNS use to higher levels. Frequency of use was mixed (depression: 8 positive, 16 nonsignificant; anxiety: 3 positive, 7 nonsignificant, among 30 studies). Number of SNS friends was mostly unrelated.
narrative_locator: Discussion, Principal Findings: 'Positive quality interactions, social support, and social connectedness most consistently related to lower levels of depression and anxiety.'
author_conclusion: SNS use correlates with depression, anxiety and wellbeing, but whether it helps or harms depends partly on the quality of social factors: positive interactions, support and connectedness are protective; negative interactions, social comparison and problematic use are risks.
rob_tool_used: Three risk of bias indicators adapted from the Cochrane risk of bias tool (reliable and valid measures; external measurement criterion for mental health; sample description including SNS activity statistics), summed 0 to 6; studies scoring 3 or above excluded

amstar2.notes: 1: SNS use as exposure, depression and anxiety as outcomes, population unrestricted, no explicit comparator. 4: eight databases including IEEE Xplore conference papers, search terms in Figure 1, 2005 limit justified; English, peer-reviewed or conference only, grey literature excluded, no reference list searching. 5: two raters screened abstracts; full texts reviewed by first and third authors. 6: who extracted data not stated. 8: Multimedia Appendix 1 (not in text file) summarizes year, population, SNS type, variables, moderators. 9: rated N because the adapted tool assesses measurement and sample reporting only; judgment call. 13: high-bias studies excluded; retrospective self-report bias discussed. 14: mixed results explained by design (ESM vs retrospective survey), moderators, observed vs self-reported data.

extraction_notes: Search date not reported; publication window January 2005 to June 2016. Only the frequency-of-use counts are printed as numbers; k left null because the 30 studies examined frequency with depression and/or anxiety and per-outcome denominators are not reported. One study found a significant negative association between Facebook-specific social anxiety and frequency (single study, not recorded). Other themes cite studies without printed counts (social comparison as risk factor for depression and anxiety; negative interaction quality with depression; problematic SNS use with depression and anxiety; number of friends mostly unrelated; social support and connectedness protective); Multimedia Appendix 2 (main results table) is not in the text file, so these appear only in the narrative. Single-study results not recorded: 41.9% of adolescents with Facebook addiction; Facebook use reduced depressive symptoms in treatment-resistant MDD; negative interactions predicted thwarted belongingness (suicidal desire risk); depressive symptoms as risk factor for Facebook peer victimization. Outcomes outside the condition list (loneliness, self-esteem, life satisfaction, well-being, negative affect) not recorded. 9 studies excluded for bias score of 3 or above.

online_exposures: frequency and time spent on TikTok
distressing content and mental health misinformation on TikTok
population_notes: Community (non-clinical) samples, mostly university students and young adults; also adolescents (10-19, eighth graders, Saudi teenagers 12-19) and general adult samples (Finland mean age 46.67). 14 countries; China 45.8% of participants.
primary_designs: 19 cross-sectional, 2 longitudinal, 2 mixed methods, 1 experimental, 2 qualitative
narrative_summary: No pooled or counted results for depression or anxiety. The review states that frequent or problematic TikTok use was closely linked with higher anxiety and depression symptoms, especially in users under 24, based on individual cross-sectional studies; one study found no direct correlation between anxiety and TikTok usage. Direction unclear (reverse causation discussed).
narrative_locator: Discussion: 'multiple studies showing a clear link between excessive engagement on the platform and increased levels of anxiety, depression, and stress'
author_conclusion: Problematic TikTok use is linked to anxiety, depression and procrastination, particularly in younger and vulnerable users; digital and media literacy, caregiver mediation and usage limits are recommended, with longitudinal and interventional research needed.
rob_tool_used: JBI checklist (cross-sectional), Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (longitudinal), CASP qualitative checklist, MMAT (mixed methods), Cochrane risk of bias tool named as RoB 2 (experimental study)

amstar2.notes: Item 2 PY: OSF registration (osf.io/cjf97), deviations not discussed. Item 4 PY: five databases, keywords, reference lists, no language limits, but grey literature excluded without justification. Item 6 Y: two reviewers extracted with a standardized form, disagreements resolved (independence implied, not explicit). Item 9 Y: design-appropriate named tools, though the RoB table for the experiment uses original Cochrane RoB domains. Item 13 Y: higher-risk studies flagged for cautious interpretation; self-report and cross-sectional limits discussed.

funding: No external funding was received for this review.
conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
extraction_notes: Only pooled figure is a 'pooled prevalence of TikTok use' of 80.19% (8141/10 154), a descriptive share of participants using TikTok, not a counted condition (most included studies sampled only TikTok users); not recorded as a finding. Abstract's 85.4% for ages 18-29 is not found in the body text. Abstract's '67.3% of such cases found among female university students' appears to come from the Smith et al. sample (67.3% female), likely a misreading. Conclusion says 11 062 participants vs 11 462 elsewhere; China share 45.8% (Results) vs 45.5% (Limitations). Barry et al. is called cross-sectional in the text but experimental in Table 1; text claims 12% depression and 15% anxiety increases after 20 min that Table 2 does not report. Barry rated overall low risk despite two High domains; Yao NOS scored '8 out of 10'. Counted conditions touched only by single studies: hazardous alcohol use and problem gambling (Savolainen), body image (Auf). Outcomes outside the condition list: stress, loneliness, FOMO, boredom, self-esteem, life satisfaction, procrastination. Liu et al. (2020) concerns general media exposure, not TikTok specifically.

online_exposures: COVID-19 news obtained on social media
population_notes: Young people (sample mean age 10-24; ages sampled 6-39), mostly university students; one primary/secondary school sample (Palestine, 6-18) and one non-student young adult sample; community samples during COVID-19 lockdowns; 7 countries (China 5 studies, USA 3, Brazil, Egypt, Canada, Palestine, Iran).
primary_designs: 12 cross-sectional, 1 longitudinal (ecological momentary assessment)

findings.label: Greater COVID-19 news consumption associated with decline in mental health (11 of 13 studies)
findings.condition: mental health (depression, anxiety, stress, distress outcomes combined)
findings.online_side: COVID-19 news consumption (social media, online and traditional sources)
findings.direction: online exposure linked to condition outcome
findings.locator: Abstract, Results: 'Increased consumption of COVID-19 news was associated with a decline in mental health ( n = 11).'

narrative_summary: Of 13 studies, 11 linked greater COVID-19 news consumption to poorer mental health. Seven measured depression and 10 anxiety. Results were more consistent for news from social media than traditional media; several studies found no association with depression. One study linked information uncertainty to acute stress disorder.
narrative_locator: Section 4 Discussion: 'The negative psychological impact for news obtained on social media is demonstrated in the reviewed literature'
author_conclusion: The literature supports an association between greater COVID-19 news consumption and poorer mental health in young people, more consistently for social media news; longitudinal designs, ecological momentary assessment and validated news-consumption measures are needed.
rob_tool_used: Adapted Q-SSP checklist (Protogerou and Hagger 2020, quality of survey studies in psychology), applied by one reviewer

amstar2.notes: Rated as a meta-analysis because a random-effects meta-analysis (anxiety prevalence, 3 studies) was performed; if that analysis is treated as outside the review question and items 11, 12 and 15 set to NA, overall would be Low. Item 2 PY: protocol posted to PsyArXiv on 4 May 2021, after the 24 April 2021 search; the added meta-analysis is disclosed as a deviation. Item 4 PY: three databases, search string (Appendix A), reference lists; English-only and peer-reviewed restrictions not justified; no grey literature. Item 9 Y: named survey-quality tool, single assessor. Item 11 Y: random effects, I2 and Q reported.

extraction_notes: The only pooled estimate is anxiety prevalence, not paired with an online exposure, so not recorded as a finding: moderate-severe anxiety 39.1% (36.7%-41.6%), N = 1395, 3 studies, I2 = 17.3%, Q (df = 2) = 3.00, p = .223, vs pre-COVID adult norm 9% (7.6%-10.4%) (Table 2); added at peer reviewer request, not in protocol. The 'n = 11' count appears only in the abstract. Exposure includes traditional media; only part of it is online. Section 3.2 says ten studies used validated mental health measures; Discussion says n = 12. Ghazawy contributes N = 534 to the meta-analysis vs a sample of 1335; spelled 'Ghazaway' in Table 2. Acute stress disorder and secondary traumatic stress may map to PTSD and trauma (lead reviewer to decide). Stress, psychological distress, somatisation and psychological health are outside the condition list. No funding or conflict statements appear in the text.

findings.label: Online peer support better than comparison at post-intervention in 2 of 4 RCTs/randomized trials (anxiety and tobacco; not depression or eating disorders)
findings.condition: mental health problems (depression and anxiety, psychological problems, eating disorders, tobacco use)
findings.online_side: online peer-to-peer support (Internet support groups, forums, virtual reality chat)
findings.direction: online exposure linked to condition outcome

findings.locator: Discussion, Principal Findings: 'Overall, two of the 4 RCTs/randomized trials yielded a positive effect for the peer-support group relative to the comparison group at post-intervention'

narrative_summary: Six studies. Two of 4 RCTs/randomized trials showed online peer support beat the comparison at post-intervention (anxiety; tobacco abstinence). No evidence of effect for depressive symptoms or eating disorders; in the remaining four studies peer support was not effective. Studies were of low quality (mean 4.6 of 9).
narrative_locator: Discussion, Principal Findings: 'There was no evidence that peer-to-peer support was effective for eating disorder or depressive symptoms'
author_conclusion: High-quality studies of online peer-to-peer support for young people are lacking; because peer support is often an adjunct to Internet interventions, its effectiveness as a stand-alone intervention urgently needs testing.

findings.online_side: digital detox (break from social media or smartphone use)
findings.direction: online exposure linked to condition outcome
findings.locator: Results, Health and well-being, Depression: 'All three studies found a significant decline in depression symptoms after a break from social media use or smartphone use in general.'

findings.online_side: digital detox (break from smartphone, SNS or texting)
findings.direction: online exposure linked to condition outcome
findings.locator: Results, Health and well-being, Anxiety: 'Only one study (Liao, 2019) found a decrease in anxiety for participants with mild–moderate anxiety symptoms after the intervention compared with the baseline assessment'

narrative_summary: All 3 studies measuring depression found a significant decline in depressive symptoms after a social media or smartphone break; 1 of 4 studies found reduced anxiety (only with mild-moderate symptoms), the other three no effect. Craving and withdrawal rose in all 3 studies assessing them; most other outcomes were mixed.
narrative_locator: Conclusion: 'digital detox interventions exert some promising effects on usage itself and on depression symptoms'
author_conclusion: Digital detox effects are mixed across outcomes; there are promising effects on use and depressive symptoms, but inconsistent and sometimes negative effects elsewhere, so no recommendation can be made; higher-quality research on moderators and mediators is needed.

narrative_summary: Qualitative synthesis of 13 studies of young people with lived ED experience. All 13 described using online ED content to compare themselves with others, often triggering negative emotions and weight-loss behaviours, though comparisons in recovery were sometimes positive. Eleven of 13 described online communities as refuge from offline isolation; communities were a double-edged sword of support and harm.
narrative_locator: Discussion, Summary of findings and cross cutting themes, p. 12: 'This synthesis of 13 studies of participants with direct experience of an eating disorder, disordered eating or eating difficulties identifies diverse practices of comparing'
author_conclusion: Online ED content is double-edged for young people with lived ED experience: comparing, curating and community can support recovery or trigger harm; lack of offline support drives use; professionals should routinely explore online platforms' role in recovery.

narrative_summary: Among 61 news articles with coded outcomes, suicide death was most frequent (35/61), then psychiatric hospitalization (12/61); suicide attempt 2/61, self-harm 1/61. narrative_summary: Of 14 studies, all 5 examining negative symptoms found higher social media use linked to lower negative symptoms and better functioning; of 8 on positive symptoms or paranoia, none reported worsening (5 no association; 2 longitudinal showed reduced paranoia). narrative_summary: Nine heterogeneous studies; no counts or pooled results. FEP case reports described misinterpretation of online communication, referential ideas, erotomanic delusions and cyberstalking linked to social media; cross-sectional studies linked Facebook or internet addiction and affect-driven immersion with schizotypal traits; one study found search results delaying care slightly outnumbered those facilitating it. Effects appeared both supportive and adverse.
narrative_locator: Discussion, section 4: 'Across the included studies, social media use was associated with both potentially supportive and potentially adverse outcomes.'
author_conclusion: Social media may act as an environmental stressor in early psychosis, but interactions are complex and context-dependent, with both supportive and adverse effects; correlational and case-based evidence prevents causal conclusions; longitudinal and qualitative studies are needed.

population_notes: People with a confirmed diagnosis of psychosis (FEP youth and chronic psychotic disorders; one trial of mothers with schizophrenia); mixed caregiver or other-condition samples (incl. mild intellectual disability) reported for the psychosis sample only; mean age 20.3-47.0; US 6, Australia 3, Canada 1, Netherlands 1.

narrative_summary: No pooled results. Early small uncontrolled studies suggested OSN interventions reduced social isolation or loneliness, but none of the controlled studies (5 RCTs) showed significant effects on social isolation or quality of life; the 5 studies reporting quality of life found no demonstrable improvement. Engagement with social features exceeded non-social features in 4 of 5 studies reporting engagement.
narrative_locator: Discussion: 'Despite these variations, none of the studies employing a control group demonstrated significant results in measures relating to social isolation or quality of life outcomes.'
author_conclusion: Higher-quality, longer-term studies did not support current purpose-built online social networking interventions for reducing social isolation or improving quality of life in psychosis; future research might promote safe use of mainstream platforms.

population_notes: Swedish context only; people with ID (study descriptors: adolescents, young people, youths, young adults) plus parents, social care staff, managers and municipal politicians; 17 peer-reviewed primary studies published 2008-2023.

narrative_summary: Across 17 Swedish studies (no counts given), people with ID had limited internet access and lower access to smartphones and computers than non-disabled people; barriers were inaccessible design, cognitive and motor demands, lacking staff support and guidelines, and restrictions by parents and staff. People with ID viewed the internet positively; staff were pessimistic. Hate comments, threats and bullying were reported.
narrative_locator: Results and Analysis, 'The Swedish Digital Intellectual Disability Divide', Digital divide (p. 514): 'They have significantly lower access to smartphones and computers, and are less active on the internet, than abled people'
author_conclusion: People with ID in Sweden have insufficient internet access; a digital disability divide and design and digital inequalities stem from societal structures, technology design and organisational conditions, not only impairment; equal structural support and policy are needed.

narrative_summary: Adults with ID used SM with positive social outcomes. Negative impacts: past cyberbullying (two papers), insults and threats, financial and sexual exploitation and social rejection (several papers; unclear if actual or feared); one study found no excess cyberbullying versus non-disabled peers. Access barriers: inaccessible platform design (four studies), lacking technical skills (six), technology cost.

author_conclusion: Adults with intellectual disabilities use SM with benefits for inclusion and identity; some know techniques to avoid exploitation and bullying; supporters need skills balancing autonomy and safety; access barriers and people with severe disabilities need further research.

population_notes: Public sector services using BWCs: law enforcement (43 studies; police, prison guards, traffic wardens), healthcare (8; physicians, clinical staff, paramedics, family carers), transport (1; railway staff). Only 2 studies on mental health inpatient wards (both UK). Mostly USA and UK; also Turkey, Uruguay, Canada.
primary_designs: Range of designs including RCTs, cluster RCTs, quasi-experimental, cohort, cross-sectional and qualitative studies (per-study designs in Appendix A, no summary counts given); not all studies reported design. Both mental health studies quasi-experimental.
narrative_summary: Only 2 of 52 studies examined BWCs on mental health inpatient wards (both UK, poor quality, cameras supplied free by the manufacturer). Results were mixed: descriptive ward-level increases and decreases in verbal abuse, violence and restraint, and a non-significant overall decrease in incidents with ward-specific changes in seriousness. Authors found no generalisable evidence that BWCs reduce patient violence.
narrative_locator: Results, Outcomes in healthcare sector, Mental health: 'Despite the low-quality research and mixed findings, both studies report that BWCs are acceptable, beneficial, and effective tools in a mental health setting.'
author_conclusion: The evidence base for BWCs in public sector services is poor; there is limited, low-quality evidence that BWCs control violence on mental health wards, and their use raises power and coercion concerns; patient-inclusive research on benefits and harms is needed.

population_notes: People living with ALS/MND (one study also carers), studied mainly via content analysis of posts on discussion forums, PatientsLikeMe and Twitter; one asynchronous online focus group of AAC users (age 35-76). Countries: Netherlands, UK, Australia, USA, several unknown. Peer-reviewed, English-language studies.
primary_designs: 9 qualitative (content analysis most frequent; also an asynchronous online focus group, interviews, a case study)
narrative_summary: All 9 qualitative studies examined text-based asynchronous platforms. Online peer support gave people with ALS informational, network and emotional support, empowerment through supporting others, and text communication avoiding speech difficulties; profile pages and graphics helped find similar peers. Only one study reported challenges: ALS physical symptoms and AAC or technology difficulties hindering device use.
narrative_locator: Section 3.4 Key findings: 'The main successful element identified in this review was social support, including informational, network, and emotional support.' Section 3.4.1: 'Only one study reported on challenges and potential barriers of online peer support'
author_conclusion: Online peer support offers people with ALS a non-judgmental space to share experiences and emotional support, aiding adaptive coping; asynchronous text platforms suit those with speech difficulties, but ALS symptoms can hinder technology use; barriers need further research.

population_notes: Caption viewers (23 studies) and creators (9) on YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Chinese platforms; community types: DHH 19, language learners 6, public 6, no identification 5, neurodivergent 4, other disabilities 4; participants mostly USA (9) and China (3), others one each (Canada, Saudi Arabia, Poland, Australia, Cyprus, South Korea).

primary_designs: 36 empirical papers (2 also datasets, 4 artifacts); data collection: semi-structured interviews 17, social media video data analysis 10, surveys 7, focus groups 3
narrative_summary: Across 36 papers (19 involving DHH communities), researchers overwhelmingly emphasized captions as the primary means for DHH viewers to participate in social media video; automatic and auto-translated captions show systemic errors, user-generated captions are inconsistent, non-speech information is sparse, sign-language captioning is nearly absent, and DHH viewers skip uncaptioned videos. ADHD viewers use captions for focus.
narrative_locator: Section 5.3.2, SMVC's Benefits to Viewers: 'Researchers overwhelmingly emphasized that captions are a primary means for DHH viewers to participate in these digital spaces'
author_conclusion: Captions on social media video operate as collective infrastructure co-produced by viewers, creators and platforms; DHH, neurodivergent and multilingual viewers depend on them while creators lack tool support, so the authors propose Participatory Captioning and note remaining research gaps.

Paper inconsistencies: Results says plans and NSSI had 'too few effects (k = 10 and k = 3, respectively)', order reversed relative to Table 2 (plans k 10, NSSI k 3); I2 recorded as the text assigns it (NSSI 70.53%, plans 95.44%). extraction_notes: Narrative synthesis (SWiM); no pooled, median, range, or study-count result is stated for any counted condition, so findings is empty. Headline depression 90% and anxiety 87% (abstract, highlights, Discussion 4.2, Conclusions) are attributed to 'certain cohorts' [43, 52] and cannot be found in any table: Table 4 gives depression 69.6% and anxiety 56.6% in victims (Skilbred-Fjeld 2020 [52]). Suicide attempts 19.0% vs 3.0% and self-harm 28.9% vs 15.2% are presented as review-level results in the abstract but come from a single study (Table 4). Autism victimization 64.1-68.9% is a single study (Accardo 2025 [43]); Section 3.4 misprints it as '64.1% to 8.9%'. Not recorded because not condition-specific: median cyber-victimization prevalence 19.1% from 27 data points (range 2.1% to 88.0%) and perpetration range 1.1% to 55.6%. Section 3.4 gives the Gianesini (2015) maximum as 63.7% but Table 3 gives 67.7%. Inclusion window 2015-2025 yet Chang 2013 and Smokowski 2014 are included. Country counts conflict (China and Taiwan 8, US 7, Spain 3 vs US and China 7, Spain 4). Total sample reported only as 'exceeded 240,000', so n left null. 2024 search strings were title-only. Abbreviations list defines PEO as 'Population, Intervention, Outcome'. PTSD and substance use mentioned without figures. Outcomes outside the condition list not recorded: stress, social isolation, anger, sadness, humiliation, fear, bystander distress. No disability-general data despite the map cell.

extraction_notes: Abstract only. Four separate meta-analyses; k and n are per meta-analysis and counted as samples, not studies; total numbers of studies and participants across the review are not reported, so totals left null. Negative Hedges' g and Fisher's Z indicate poorer body image. The g = -0.12 result compares higher- vs lower-risk contextual features, not exposure vs control, and the g = -0.68 result has p = .05. Outlier-removed estimates described only as smaller but significant. CIs, heterogeneity, model, publication bias, risk of bias tool, search date, and participant ages are not in the abstract.
